content: Phosphorus burns are uncommon in typical clinical settings and are primarily observed in military and industrial environments. Despite their rarity, these burns can be life-threatening, even when the affected area is small, and they are often associated with extended hospital stays. The objective of this review was to evaluate the evidence regarding the effects, both beneficial and harmful, of various interventions used to treat phosphorus burns. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in October 2013 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid OLDMEDLINE, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, EBSCO CINAHL, and the Conference Proceedings Citation Index Science (CPCI-S). No restrictions were applied regarding study design, language, publication date, or publication status. The review included any studies comparing different methods of managing phosphorus burns, with a focus on randomised trials but not limited to them. Two non-randomised comparative studies were identified, both of which examined the outcomes of patients treated with and without the use of copper sulphate. The findings from these two studies do not support the use of copper sulphate in the management of phosphorus burns. In fact, the limited evidence available suggests that copper sulphate may be harmful. Specifically, systemic absorption of copper sulphate has been associated with potential adverse effects, and there is no evidence to suggest that its use improves the visualisation or removal of phosphorus particles, nor does it lead to better clinical outcomes. The recommended first aid for phosphorus burns involves prompt and practical measures, including the immediate removal of the patient’s clothing, continuous irrigation of the wound(s) with water or saline, and the removal of phosphorus particles. There is no evidence to justify the use of copper sulphate as part of this process. At present, no other relevant comparisons have been identified to guide the management of phosphorus burns beyond these initial measures. Future updates of this review will consider evidence from articles published in languages other than English, as they may provide additional insights into treatment comparisons.
